dimensions.name: Spec decoding & S3/SigV4 fidelity research

evidence.note: Wrote durable reference notes (MEMORY.md, halyard-runtime.md) capturing the runtime/contract before implementing — building a persistent reference of the spec.

Task breakdown systematically inventories the full contract: a dedicated SigV4 task (step 22) explicitly names header- and query-signing, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, clock skew, and access-key->tenant resolution; other tasks cover pinned semantics, tenant status matrix, console data-testids (26), and admin JSON schemas (25).
sigv4.py authored as a standalone module ahead of endpoint wiring, showing the hardest canonicalization part was treated as a discrete concern rather than inlined blindly.

Probed real boto3 behavior — inspected headers boto3 actually sends on PutObject and forced/unit-tested chunked (aws-chunked) upload dechunking — grounding canonicalization against ground truth rather than assuming.
Tested presigned expiry/tampering against real signed requests and fixed sigv4.py accordingly, validating query-signing behavior late in the build.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it enumerates operations, error codes, and the tenant/console/admin contract in a structured breakdown and explicitly isolates the SigV4 hard parts (query-signing, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, clock skew) plus maintains durable reference notes. It reaches into anchor-8 territory by probing real boto3 (header inspection, forced chunked uploads, presigned tamper tests) rather than purely assuming. It falls short of a full 8/10 because much of that boto3 canonicalization probing is reactive debugging rather than upfront grounding, and there's no visible capture of real signed requests before coding sigv4.py. That places the observed behavior at a 7.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & verifiable milestones

evidence.note: Seven explicit TaskCreate milestones forming a dependency-ordered hierarchy: foundation/storage substrate + audit + tenant seeding first, then SigV4 auth, then data-plane CRUD/multipart/versioning, then policy/notifications/lifecycle, then admin+console API, then console SPA, then a final boto3 test/fix task. Correct foundational-before-dependent ordering, subsystems treated as discrete units.
Milestones marked in_progress then completed in sequence across the entire build, showing a coherent map sustained over the whole horizon rather than abandoned early planning.

Console UI built (task 6) and verified via a dedicated Playwright browser-test track, distinct from the boto3 correctness track (steps 92-150) — the two grading surfaces are scoped as separate tracks.

SigV4 exactness and concurrency (highest-uncertainty foundations) were only exercised by acceptance tests after essentially all code was written, and the entire data plane was lumped into one task rather than gated incrementally — falling short of risk-ordered, per-milestone acceptance checks (anchors 8/10).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced an explicit, dependency-sequenced milestone hierarchy (steps 21-27) with foundational auth/storage before dependent features and the console scoped as its own track, and it tracked those milestones to completion across the whole trajectory — clearly above anchor 5 and approaching 8. It stops short of a full 8/10 because there is no stated per-milestone 'done' check (verification was a lumped final task, and the data plane was one omnibus task rather than gated as 'PUT/GET signed before multipart'), and the highest-risk foundations (SigV4, concurrency) were built-then-tested rather than proven earliest, so the level lands at 7.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & the DOM contract

evidence.note: Wrote and ran a real boto3 test suite (test_s3.py), used failures to drive fixes (head_object), and built devrestart.sh to re-run cleanly — genuine boto3 round-trip verification.
test_concurrency.py exercises the 30-client requirement, plus explicit audit-log inspection and auth-failure audit logging — concurrency + audit atomicity checks.
test_lifecycle_worker.py run with fast-clock settings via a dedicated devrestart_lc.sh, mirroring the grader's S3CLONE_LIFECYCLE_SECONDS_PER_DAY=1 condition.
Installed Playwright + system chromium and wrote test_browser.py to verify console DOM/testids and visible side-effects, not just API responses.
Forced boto3 chunked/UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD upload, verified error codes/XML content-type, tested presigned expiry & tampering, and killed the worker to confirm respawn — grader-condition edge cases.
Multiple full regression re-runs across all suites, marking subsystems complete only after tests passed — repeated regression catching.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built a comprehensive, per-subsystem verification suite (boto3 data-plane, admin, console browser/testid, concurrency, notifications, audit) and specifically reproduced grader conditions the level-8 anchor names plus the level-10 extras: presigned/UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD signing, lifecycle expiry with the fast-clock env var, audit under concurrency, and real browser DOM checks. It re-ran full regressions repeatedly and gated subsystem completion on green tests, matching the level-10 description; I land at 9 because the checks are a suite of separate test files run repeatedly rather than an explicitly unified reusable harness.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Up-front decomposition into 7 subsystem-level tasks (foundation, SigV4, S3 ops, policy/notify/lifecycle, admin+console API, console SPA, testing) — a spec-derived running checklist covering the whole surface.
TaskUpdate marks each subsystem complete only after its dedicated test phase passes, giving an accurate done-vs-remaining picture sustained across the horizon.

Admin-test failure isolated via targeted probes ('test qt creation directly', 'fix test name and rerun') rather than blind re-runs — evidence of detecting and closing a specific issue instead of circling.

Systematic late hardening pass touching individual spec items (error codes+XML type, worker respawn, persistence, presigned tampering, regression) — implicit cross-check against the enumerated surface, but not tracked as an explicit per-code/per-testid map.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained an accurate subsystem-level checklist (TaskCreate/TaskUpdate) and reliably marked tasks off only after their verification passed, with no sign of losing the plot or believing the build complete while a family was missing — matching the level-5 anchor. Targeted (non-circular) debugging and a systematic spec-family verification sweep push it above 5, but the tracking granularity stays coarse (7 tasks, no explicit per-error-code/per-testid coverage map or partially-done annotations), so it falls short of the level-8 anchor. That places the observed level at 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: head_object test failed; agent Read the source, Grep'd the exact branch (`if head:`), made a targeted Edit, then restarted and retested — investigation-before-fix, not a random tweak.
Recognized it was testing a stale gunicorn process and wrote devrestart.sh for clean restarts — corrected the verification setup itself, a meta-level fix that unblocked accurate diagnosis.
Admin tests failed; agent dumped full output, tested tenant creation in isolation, and 'fixed test name' — diagnosed the failure lay in the test rather than blindly patching product code.

Large-PUT corruption traced to chunked transfer-encoding: agent inspected the exact headers boto3 sends, implemented dechunking, searched for ALL get_data call sites to propagate the fix (192), unit-tested dechunk in isolation, then verified with a forced real boto3 chunked upload — root-cause diagnosis plus cross-call-site propagation and new verification.
Presigned expiry/tampering probe failed; agent Read sigv4.py, made a focused Edit, and retested presigned expiry — targeted SigV4 correction rather than superficial retry.

dimensions.reasoning: Across multiple hard mismatches (head semantics, chunked-encoding body corruption, admin test failures, presigned SigV4) the agent consistently investigated the true cause — reading source, inspecting exactly what boto3 sends, isolating whether the fault was in test or product — before making a targeted fix and re-verifying, matching anchor 8. The chunked-encoding episode goes further: it propagated the fix across all get_data call sites and added an isolated unit test plus a forced-chunked boto3 check, reaching toward 9. It stops short of 10 because there is no visible updating of the plan/verification to structurally prevent a whole class of recurrence, and the summary-only trajectory limits confidence.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across the split grader

evidence.note: Planning phase created a dedicated task for the console SPA enumerating all required data-testids, confirm dialog, and secret-reveal modal — the browser-graded surface is acknowledged as a first-class deliverable up front, not an afterthought.
Built the full console (index.html, app.js, styles.css) rather than leaving the UX surface as an API-only stub.

Installed Playwright and wrote/ran an actual browser UI test to verify the console DOM behavior the way the automated browser grader would — real verification effort invested in the console-worth-half surface, going beyond stub level.

The large majority of iteration went into data-plane correctness (boto3 round-trips, chunked encoding, error codes, concurrency, persistence, presigned edge cases), showing the correctness stage secured but consuming most cycles; no visible explicit 50/50 budget reasoning or rebalancing.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent allocated genuine, verified effort to both surfaces — planning a dedicated console task with all testids, building the full console, and browser-testing it — which clears the level-5 bar (neither surface a stub) and reaches into level-8 territory by defending the console's required views/testids/side-effects while securing core data-plane correctness. It falls short of a clean 8 because there is no observable explicit reasoning about the 50/50 weighting or dynamic rebalancing, and the console reached its passing bar in a comparatively brief span while data-plane correctness dominated the iteration budget. This places the observed behavior at 7, between the level-5 and level-8 anchors.

rubric.task_read: This is an extremely large, long-horizon build: a multi-tenant S3-compatible object store spanning SigV4 auth (byte-exact against boto3), a broad data plane (multipart, versioning, ranged reads, conditional ops, policies, notifications, lifecycle), an admin JSON API, an audit log, a background lifecycle worker, concurrency guarantees, and a browser-verified web console with a precise DOM contract. Difficulty comes from breadth (many loosely-coupled subsystems), unforgiving exactness (SigV4 signatures, pinned ETag/error semantics, load-bearing data-testids), and a split grader (binary correctness stage + UX rubric worth half). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in orientation, sequencing, self-built verification, and progress tracking — over-investment is hard to reach here; the risk is thrash and lost threads.

dimensions.name: Spec decoding & S3/SigV4 fidelity research
dimensions.description: Extracting the exact contract from a dense spec and grounding the AWS-compatible behaviors (SigV4 canonicalization, pinned ETag/error/status semantics, boto3 quirks) before and while coding.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The correctness stage is binary and byte-exact against boto3; a misread of SigV4 rules, the multipart ETag formula, presigned/UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD handling, or the cross-tenant status matrix silently fails whole test families. Blind coding here is fatal.

anchors.0: Starts implementing endpoints with no attempt to catalog the spec's requirements or understand SigV4/boto3 behavior.
anchors.3: Skims the spec and codes from memory; treats SigV4 and the error/status matrix as things to guess at, discovering gaps only when tests fail.
anchors.5: Enumerates the required operations and error codes, and correctly researches the core hard parts (SigV4 canonical request/signing, path-style routing) before implementing them.
anchors.8: Systematically inventories the full contract (auth modes, pinned ETag/range/error semantics, tenant status matrix, console DOM testids, admin schemas) and probes real boto3 behavior to nail canonicalization edge cases (UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, query-signing, clock skew) rather than assuming.
anchors.10: Builds a durable reference of the exact contract and continuously validates ambiguous behaviors against ground truth (e.g. capturing real boto3 signed requests, confirming header casing/encoding), resolving under-specified corners with evidence and revisiting them as new subsystems expose new interactions.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & verifiable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking the build into an ordered hierarchy of independently-checkable subsystems (auth core → bucket/object CRUD → multipart/versioning → policies/notifications/lifecycle → admin/audit → console) with a defensible dependency order.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There are ~10 loosely-coupled subsystems plus two grading surfaces. Without milestone structure and a sane order (auth and storage substrate first, since everything depends on them), the agent risks half-finishing many pieces and passing none of the binary stage.

anchors.0: No decomposition; codes in an undifferentiated stream with no notion of stages or completion criteria.
anchors.3: A vague or flat to-do list that mixes trivial and load-bearing items, with no dependency ordering and no per-item definition of done.
anchors.5: Clear list of the major subsystems tackled in a reasonable order (foundational auth/storage before dependent features), each treated as a discrete unit.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with correct dependency sequencing and a stated 'done' check per milestone (e.g. 'boto3 can PUT/GET a signed object' before layering multipart), and the two grading surfaces scoped as separate tracks.
anchors.10: Milestones are risk-ordered so the highest-uncertainty foundations (SigV4 exactness, concurrent storage substrate) are proven earliest, each with a concrete acceptance check, and the plan is re-partitioned as reality reveals coupling — sustaining a coherent map across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & the DOM contract
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks — boto3 round-trips, curl/HTTP probes, concurrency stress, console DOM/testid checks — beyond the hidden grader, rather than assuming code works.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is binary and hidden; the console is browser-verified against exact data-testids. The only way to know a subsystem passes is to reproduce the grader's conditions locally. Unverified subsystems are effectively untested until they silently fail.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints work because they were written.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual pokes at a couple of endpoints; no boto3 round-trip, no concurrency check, no console DOM verification.
anchors.5: Uses real boto3 to exercise the main data-plane operations and hits the admin/console APIs directly, catching obvious breakage.
anchors.8: Systematic verification per subsystem: boto3 round-trips for edge cases (multipart ETag, ranged 206/416, conditional/precondition, cross-tenant status codes), a concurrency test for the 30-client requirement, and console checks that assert the required testids and side-effects.
anchors.10: Builds a reusable verification harness that mirrors grader conditions across all subsystems (including presigned/UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD signing, notification webhook delivery/retry, lifecycle expiry with the fast-clock env var, audit-line atomicity under concurrency), runs it repeatedly to catch regressions, and treats a subsystem as done only when its checks are green.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which of the many subsystems/operations/error-codes are done, in progress, or untouched, and detecting stalls or circular debugging.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of operations and error codes across two grading surfaces over a long horizon, it is easy to lose the plot — believing the build is near-complete while whole families (e.g. notifications, lifecycle, a console view) are missing or half-done.

anchors.0: No sense of what's done vs remaining; repeatedly rediscovers or re-touches the same areas.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; loses track of which error codes/operations remain and drifts between areas without closure.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystems/operations and marks them off as completed, giving a roughly accurate done-vs-remaining view.
anchors.8: Granular, maintained tracking down to individual operations, error codes, and console testids, with explicit recognition when a subsystem is only partially done and when a debugging effort is going in circles.
anchors.10: Sustains an accurate coverage map across the entire horizon, cross-checked against the spec's enumerated surface (every error code, every notification event, every admin route, every testid), and reliably surfaces stuck/thrashing states early enough to redirect effort instead of grinding.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising approach when a verification fails or a boto3/SigV4 assumption is disproven, rather than repeatedly patching a broken model.
dimensions.why_it_matters: SigV4 and byte-exact behaviors are notorious for subtle mismatches; the agent will hit failing signatures and mismatched status codes. Progress depends on diagnosing the true cause and revising, not re-trying superficial fixes on a wrong mental model.

anchors.0: Ignores failures or keeps making the same change; barrels ahead on assumptions already shown false.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with random tweaks and no root-cause reasoning; abandons hard subsystems instead of correcting course.
anchors.5: When a check fails, investigates the cause and makes a targeted fix, adjusting the approach for that subsystem.
anchors.8: Diagnoses failures to root cause (e.g. isolating exactly which SigV4 canonicalization step diverges from boto3), and revises the design or shared abstractions when a foundational assumption proves wrong.
anchors.10: Treats divergence as signal: pinpoints root causes with evidence, propagates the correction across all affected subsystems (not just the failing case), and updates the plan/verification so the same class of error can't recur — sustaining forward progress through repeated hard mismatches.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across the split grader
dimensions.description: Deliberately budgeting effort between the binary correctness stage and the browser-verified console UX rubric, which each contribute half the final score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The console UX is worth half the score yet is easy to under-serve while sinking unbounded time into SigV4/data-plane perfection; conversely, a polished console with a broken data plane also caps the score. Explicit allocation across the two surfaces is a task-specific meta-decision beyond generic sequencing.

anchors.0: Pours all effort into one surface (e.g. the data plane) and never meaningfully addresses the other.
anchors.3: Acknowledges both surfaces but lets one consume nearly all effort with no deliberate balancing.
anchors.5: Allocates real effort to both the correctness stage and the console, ensuring neither is left as a stub.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the 50/50 weighting and paces work so both surfaces reach a passing bar, defending the console's required views/testids and side-effects while securing core data-plane correctness.
anchors.10: Actively manages the effort budget across the horizon against the split grader — securing must-pass foundations on both surfaces first, then investing marginal effort where it yields the most score, and revisiting the balance as each surface's state becomes clear.
